pages.text: At the edge of the village stood the baobab, so wide that ten children could not reach around it. People said it whispered at night. Rabi and her brother Mumuni wanted to know why. Their grandmother, Memuna, said, “Come at dusk. We will listen together, with respect.”
sentences: At the edge of the village stood the baobab, so wide that ten children could not reach around it.
People said it whispered at night.
Rabi and her brother Mumuni wanted to know why.
Their grandmother, Memuna, said, “Come at dusk.
We will listen together, with respect.”
pages.alt: Two children and their grandmother approach a huge baobab tree in the northern savanna at dusk.

pages.text: They sat at a safe distance, on a mat. As the sky turned orange, the first whisper came: a low, breathy shhhh from the hollow in the trunk. Mumuni grabbed his sister’s arm. “It is the tree,” he whispered. “Or something inside it.”
sentences: They sat at a safe distance, on a mat.
As the sky turned orange, the first whisper came: a low, breathy shhhh from the hollow in the trunk.
Mumuni grabbed his sister’s arm.
“It is the tree,” he whispered.
“Or something inside it.”
pages.alt: A boy grips his sister’s arm as the sun sets behind the baobab.

pages.text: Rabi opened her notebook. “Let us think like scientists,” she said. “Idea one: the wind.” She held up a strip of cloth. It fluttered gently. “The wind blows across the hollow, like blowing over a bottle top.” She blew over a bottle. It hummed. Mumuni’s eyes widened.
sentences: Rabi opened her notebook.
“Let us think like scientists,” she said.
“Idea one: the wind.” She held up a strip of cloth.
It fluttered gently.
“The wind blows across the hollow, like blowing over a bottle top.” She blew over a bottle.
It hummed.
Mumuni’s eyes widened.
pages.alt: A girl holds a cloth strip and blows over a bottle while her brother watches.

pages.text: Then dark shapes poured out of the branches into the sky: fruit bats, heading off to feed. “Idea two: animals,” said Rabi. “Bats, and maybe an owl.” A pale barn owl glided out of the hollow without a sound, making the whole tree seem to breathe.
sentences: Then dark shapes poured out of the branches into the sky: fruit bats, heading off to feed.
“Idea two: animals,” said Rabi.
“Bats, and maybe an owl.” A pale barn owl glided out of the hollow without a sound, making the whole tree seem to breathe.
pages.alt: Fruit bats and a pale owl fly from a baobab against an orange sky.

pages.text: Grandma Memuna told them a story. “When I was a girl, the old people said this tree keeps the village’s memories. Elders met under it. We still do not cut it down or burn near it.” Mumuni sat up. “Is the whisper the memories?” “Perhaps,” she said. “A story can be true in a different way from a measurement.”
sentences: Grandma Memuna told them a story.
“When I was a girl, the old people said this tree keeps the village’s memories.
Elders met under it.
We still do not cut it down or burn near it.” Mumuni sat up.
“Is the whisper the memories?” “Perhaps,” she said.
“A story can be true in a different way from a measurement.”
pages.alt: The grandmother tells the children a story under the tree in the dim light.

pages.text: It grew dark. The whispers changed: now tiny taps, like fingers on a drum. Mumuni wanted to run. Rabi wanted to climb into the hollow. “No,” said Grandma Memuna gently. “Old trees can hide snakes and fall branches. We look from here. A brave person is also a careful person.”
sentences: It grew dark.
The whispers changed: now tiny taps, like fingers on a drum.
Mumuni wanted to run.
Rabi wanted to climb into the hollow.
“No,” said Grandma Memuna gently.
“Old trees can hide snakes and fall branches.
We look from here.
A brave person is also a careful person.”
pages.alt: The grandmother holds out an arm to stop the children from approaching the hollow.

pages.text: Rabi pointed her torch at the ground. Seed pods the size of a hand were dropping from the branches and tapping on the dry earth. “Idea three: falling fruit,” she wrote. “So the wind, the bats, the owl and the fruit explain the whispers.” “All of them?” asked Mumuni.
sentences: Rabi pointed her torch at the ground.
Seed pods the size of a hand were dropping from the branches and tapping on the dry earth.
“Idea three: falling fruit,” she wrote.
“So the wind, the bats, the owl and the fruit explain the whispers.” “All of them?” asked Mumuni.
pages.alt: A torch beam shows hard seed pods falling on dry ground.

pages.text: Then the wind stopped. The bats were gone. The pods stopped falling. But from deep in the hollow, one soft whisper came, so clear it sounded like words: “Rabi… Mumuni… well done.” The children stared at their grandmother. She only smiled. “Science answers many things,” she said. “And a good scientist can leave one question open.” The end.

The bats were gone.
The pods stopped falling.

She only smiled.
“Science answers many things,” she said.
“And a good scientist can leave one question open.” The end.
pages.alt: The children and grandmother sit quietly while a faint glow shimmers inside the baobab hollow.

activities.question: What was Rabi’s first idea about the whisper?
options: The wind blowing across the hollow

activities.prompt: Rabi has two ideas so far. What could she do to test the idea that falling fruit makes the tapping?
options: Look at the ground with a torch from a safe distance

activities.question: Why did Grandma Memuna say they should look from a distance?
options: Old trees can hide snakes and drop branches
It was time to go home

activities.definition: A guess that can be tested to see if it is true.

items: They listened at a safe distance.
Rabi tried the wind idea with a bottle.
She noticed the bats and the owl.
She saw the seed pods falling.

activities.prompt: Rabi learned that being brave also means being careful. When have you been brave and careful at the same time?

glossary.definition: An empty space inside something, like a tree trunk.
A very soft, quiet sound made with the breath.
Treating someone or something with care and honour.
